passage.title: A shorter working week
passage.text: When our office moved to a four-day working week, I expected every Friday to feel like a holiday. In fact, the first month was tiring: we tried to fit all our old meetings into fewer days. Then we replaced routine meetings with short written updates. I now have more time to concentrate, although urgent messages still interrupt me. I would recommend the change, but only if a team is willing to change how it works, rather than simply making each day longer. A shorter week alone does not solve poor organisation.

passage.title: A square without cars
passage.text: The council’s plan to make the central square car-free has been criticised by shopkeepers who fear losing customers. Yet the trial in the neighbouring district suggests that the effect depends less on parking spaces than on access. There, sales initially fell while confusing signs sent visitors away. After clearer routes and regular shuttle buses were introduced, trade recovered. This does not prove our square will thrive: several shops here sell bulky goods, unlike those in the trial. The sensible response is therefore neither to abandon the plan nor to declare it a guaranteed success, but to test deliveries and public transport before committing to a permanent scheme.

passage.title: What does access mean?
passage.text: The museum’s promise to digitise its entire collection has acquired an almost moral force: objections are easily portrayed as opposition to access itself. That framing obscures a more awkward question about what access means. A searchable image may reach someone who could never travel to the building, but it may also detach an object from the circumstances that make it intelligible. This is not an argument for keeping collections behind closed doors. Rather, the museum should resist counting every uploaded image as an equivalent educational gain. Digitisation can widen participation, provided that curatorial choices remain visible and resources are not diverted so completely that the surviving physical displays become an afterthought. The real measure of success is not how little remains undigitised, but how much more a visitor, online or otherwise, can understand.
